scenario: AITA for insisting that my son’s therapist tells me why my son wants to see him. | My son [17] was always a normal boy, with many friends, very active and didn’t seam to have any kind of problem. But one day we he told us he needed to go see a therapist. We were really surprised by that, we never thought he will ask us something like that. We ask him why but he didn’t want to tell us. We were worried so we send him to a therapist and now he goes once a week. In our eyes he is still the same kid that before. We tried to think about things that he may have. We thought maybe he is bulimic or anorexic ( as he is very thin ) but he isn’t that skinny and those things tend to affect women, not men. We thought of depression but that also doesn’t seem very likely. We decided that theorizing wouldn’t give us an answer so we ask his therapist and refused, saying that he couldn’t say what my son told him. I told him that we didn’t want the specifics but at least the reason why he goes to therapy. But he refused again. We try to insist many times but he didn’t give up. And the day after, our son come to us and tell us that he know that we insisted on knowing why he wants therapy ( we don’t know if the therapist told him or maybe he hear us talking about it in the house ) and insulted us. He didn’t talk to us for the rest of the day. Now, we know that insist to know wasn’t the best idea but we are his parents and we deserve to know. We really are assholes?

Pushing for details could have made him feel like he couldn’t trust you or the therapist. - His anger wasn’t just about the disclosure; it was about **feeling controlled or betrayed**. That’s a valid emotional response. 3. **Alternatives to Forcing Answers** - Instead of demanding specifics, you could have: - **Asked the therapist for general guidance**: *"What are common reasons teens seek therapy at this age?"* (This shows concern without invading privacy.) - **Approached your son with curiosity, not suspicion**: *"I’m glad you’re getting help. If you ever want to talk about it, I’m here."* This might have encouraged him to open up organically. - **Focused on the process**: Asked the therapist how therapy is progressing (e.g., *"Is he engaging positively?"*) without prying into content. 4. **The "Normal" vs. "Problem" Mindset** - Your assumption that your son "had no problems" before therapy is a common parental bias. Many issues (e.g., social anxiety, perfectionism, or existential distress) don’t manifest overtly. His thinness might relate to something unrelated to eating disorders (e.g., stress, family history, or body image pressures). - **Therapy isn’t always about "fixing" a crisis**—it can also be about self-exploration, coping skills, or navigating identity. Your son might be seeking help for something you’d never expect (e.g., career uncertainty, grief, or moral dilemmas). 5. **Long-Term Trust** - Your son’s reaction suggests a **broken trust**. If he feels you’ll exploit his vulnerability, he may avoid seeking help in the future—even if he needs it. This could have lasting consequences for his mental health. --- ### **Why You Might Still Feel Justified** - **Parental Anxiety**: It’s natural to worry when a child seeks therapy, especially if you don’t understand the reason. Your goal was to protect him, even if the method was misguided. - **Lack of Context**: Without knowing the therapist’s approach or your son’s specific issues, it’s hard to judge the therapist’s refusal as "wrong." Some therapists are strict about confidentiality to avoid coercion. - **Cultural Norms**: In some families, transparency is prioritized over privacy. However, this scenario shows that **absolute transparency can backfire** with teens. --- ### **What You Can Do Now** 1. **Apologize and Rebuild Trust**: - Acknowledge that you overstepped: *"I realize now that I shouldn’t have pushed for details. I’m sorry I made you feel judged. I’m here to support you, no matter what."* - Give him space to open up on his terms. 2. **Work with the Therapist Collaboratively**: - Ask the therapist for **general updates** (e.g., *"How is he responding to therapy?"*) without asking for specifics. Frame it as a team effort: *"We want to help him as much as possible."* 3. **Educate Yourself**: - Research common teen struggles (e.g., [Teen Mental Health](https://www.nami.org/About-Mental-Illness/Mental-Health-Conditions/Depression-in-Teens), [LGBTQ+ Youth](https://www.thetrevorproject.org/)) to understand why he might seek help. 4. **Observe Changes**: - Pay attention to subtle shifts in his behavior (e.g., mood, sleep, social interactions) rather than fixating on a single "reason." --- ### **Final Thought: Ethics of the Situation** Your insistence wasn’t *malicious*, but it was **self-centered in its approach**. The therapist’s refusal was ethically sound because: - It prioritized your son’s **autonomy and safety**. - It respected the **therapeutic relationship**, which is built on trust. - It avoided **re-traumatizing** him by forcing disclosure. You weren’t "assholes" in the sense of being intentionally harmful, but you **failed to consider the bigger picture**—your son’s emotional well-being and the dynamics of therapy. The key lesson is that **parental love isn’t about control; it’s about creating a safe space for your child to grow, even if that means not knowing every detail**.
